newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African forward rates fall as cash squeeze eases.
newsitem.headline: S.African forward rates fall as cash squeeze eases.

text.p: Signs that the December cash squeeze was beginning to loosen its grip on market liquidity pushed one-year forward rates to their lowest levels in five weeks on Wednesday.

Forward rates kicked up sharply in December, peaking at a record high of 56.25 basis points on the 18th, as the Christmas spending season neared its peak, before beginning to taper off at the beginning of January.
On Wednesday, one-year forward rates touched a 51.25 bid -- their best level since November 29 -- which translates into a rand/dollar exchange rate of about 5.18 rand twelve months from now.
Forward traders said the easing in rates was linked to an easing of pressures on the money market.
"There is anticipation that liquidity is slowly but surely creeping back into the market," Braam Verhage, chief forward dealer at First National Bank, said.
He said that forward rates had risen in December primarily as a result of the cash crunch in the seasonally tight period.

"The lack of rand liquidity made it overshoot to the extent that it did...it was extremely difficult to get hold of rands," Verhage said, noting that the money market shortage had hovered around the 10 billion rand mark for most of last month.
Evidence of an easing in liquidity has been borne out by a fall in short-term interest rates.

Twelve-month NCDs have fallen from between 17.65/35 to 17.15/05 percent currently, while call rates have eased to around 17.5 percent from 18.25 percent in December. The money market shortage has also held below the 10 billion rand mark this week.
Money market traders said that as an easing in liquidity was traditional in the first weeks of January, it was too early to tell whether the change in market conditions would be sustained.
"Basically what the forwards are saying though, is that people are expecting rates to go lower this year."
A survey conducted by Reuters last November predicted that interest rates would be cut by as much as three basis points by the end of 1997.
Bank rate -- last hiked on November 21 last year -- currently stands at 17.00 percent.
